We report on measurements of the transverse fluctuations of a string in a turbulent air jet flow. Harmonic modes are excited by the fluctuating drag force, at different wave-numbers. This simple mechanical probe makes it possible to measure excitations of the flow at specific scales, averaged over space and time: it is a scale-resolved, global measurement. We also measure the dissipation associated to the string motion, and we consider the ratio of the fluctuations over dissipation (FDR). In an exploratory approach, we investigate the concept of {\it effective temperature} defined through the FDR. We compare our observations with other definitions of temperature in turbulence. From the theory of Kolmogorov (1941), we derive the exponent -11/3 expected for the spectrum of the fluctuations. This simple model and our experimental results are in good agreement, over the range of wave-numbers, and Reynolds number accessible ($74000 \leq Re \leq 170000$).

# Transverse String Fluctuations as a Probe of Turbulent Flow

## Experimental Approach

We investigated the transverse fluctuations of a string immersed in a turbulent air jet flow. As the turbulent stream interacts with the string, the fluctuating drag force acts upon it, exciting harmonic modes at a range of different wave-numbers. By measuring these induced transverse displacements, we were able to characterize how the turbulent flow drives the mechanical response of the string across its spectrum of vibrational modes.

## A Mechanical Probe for Scale-Resolved Measurements

The string functions as a mechanical probe of the surrounding flow, offering a distinctive means of characterizing turbulent excitations. Because each harmonic mode corresponds to a specific wave-number, this approach enables scale-resolved measurements of the flow's excitations. Crucially, these measurements are global in nature: rather than sampling the flow at a single point, the string integrates the driving forces over its entire length, yielding excitation data at specific scales that are naturally averaged over both space and time. This provides a complementary perspective to conventional localized flow diagnostics.

## Dissipation and the Fluctuation-to-Dissipation Ratio

In parallel with the fluctuation measurements, we quantified the dissipation associated with the string's motion. Combining these two quantities allowed us to construct the fluctuation-to-dissipation ratio (FDR), a diagnostic inspired by equilibrium statistical mechanics. In systems at thermal equilibrium, the fluctuation-dissipation theorem relates the magnitude of fluctuations to the system's dissipative response through the temperature. By evaluating the FDR in this turbulent, far-from-equilibrium context, we were able to explore the concept of an effective temperature for turbulence and assess the extent to which such an analogy holds.

## Theoretical Framework from Kolmogorov's 1941 Theory

To interpret our results, we developed a theoretical model grounded in Kolmogorov's 1941 (K41) theory of turbulence. Starting from the established scaling relations for the energy distribution across scales in fully developed turbulence, and accounting for the coupling between the fluctuating drag force and the string's harmonic modes, we derived the expected spectral behavior of the transverse fluctuations. This analysis predicts a characteristic spectral exponent of −11/3 for the fluctuation spectrum as a function of wave-number.

## Comparison Between Theory and Experiment

Finally, we compared the predictions of our theoretical model with the experimental measurements. The two showed good agreement across the accessible ranges of wave-numbers and over a broad span of Reynolds numbers, spanning 74{,}000 ≤ Re ≤ 170{,}000. This consistency between the K41-based prediction and the observed fluctuation spectra validates the string-based mechanical probe as a reliable tool for scale-resolved turbulence measurements and lends support to the effective-temperature interpretation derived from the fluctuation-to-dissipation ratio.

# Probing Turbulent Flows with a Vibrating String: A Scale-Resolved Approach

## Introduction

Turbulence remains one of the outstanding challenges in classical physics, characterized by chaotic fluctuations spanning a wide range of spatial and temporal scales. Understanding how energy is distributed and dissipated across these scales is central to characterizing turbulent flows. In this work, we introduce a novel experimental approach that uses the transverse fluctuations of a string immersed in a turbulent air jet to probe flow excitations at specific length scales, offering a scale-resolved, global measurement of the underlying turbulence.

## Experimental Concept

The core idea of our method is to exploit a flexible string as a mechanical sensor embedded within the flow. When a string is placed transverse to a turbulent air jet, the fluctuating drag forces exerted by the turbulent eddies drive the string's harmonic modes. Each vibrational mode of the string corresponds to a distinct wave-number, and thus to a specific spatial scale of the flow. By measuring the amplitude of the string's transverse fluctuations across its various modes, we effectively sample the turbulent excitations at a series of well-defined scales.

This modal decomposition is the key advantage of the technique: rather than providing a single point measurement, the string integrates information along its length while simultaneously resolving contributions from different wave-numbers. In this sense, the string acts as a global yet scale-resolved probe of the turbulent flow.

## Effective Temperature and the Fluctuation-Dissipation Framework

To interpret the string's response, we adopt a statistical-mechanical framework centered on the fluctuation-dissipation relationship. In equilibrium systems, the fluctuation-dissipation theorem connects the spontaneous fluctuations of a quantity to the system's dissipative response to external perturbations, with temperature setting the proportionality. In a driven, non-equilibrium system such as a turbulent flow, this relationship no longer holds in its equilibrium form, but one can define an **effective temperature** through the ratio of measured fluctuations to measured dissipation.

In our experiments, we characterized both the transverse fluctuations of the string (its spontaneous, turbulence-driven motion) and its dissipation properties. By combining these two measurements, we constructed an effective temperature that encapsulates the strength of turbulent forcing at each accessible scale. This provides a physically meaningful way to quantify how energy from the turbulent cascade couples into the string's mechanical degrees of freedom.

## Theoretical Model and Spectral Prediction

To predict the behavior of the string's fluctuation spectrum, we developed a model grounded in Kolmogorov's classical theory of turbulence. Kolmogorov's phenomenology describes the inertial range of turbulence through a universal energy cascade, in which energy is transferred from large to small scales with a characteristic scaling behavior. By convolving the statistics of the fluctuating drag forces—derived from the Kolmogorov energy spectrum—with the mechanical response of the string's harmonic modes, our model predicts a specific power-law dependence of the fluctuation spectrum on wave-number.

The central prediction of this model is a **spectral exponent of -11/3**. This value emerges naturally from combining the -5/3 Kolmogorov scaling of the velocity fluctuations with the additional wave-number dependence introduced by the string's modal response and the drag-force coupling. The -11/3 exponent therefore represents a distinctive signature that connects the observable string dynamics directly to the underlying structure of the turbulent cascade.

## Results

We tested this prediction across a range of experimental conditions, systematically varying the flow to span Reynolds numbers from 74,000 to 170,000. Throughout this range, and across the full span of accessible wave-numbers, the measured fluctuation spectra exhibited excellent agreement with the predicted -11/3 power law. The robustness of this agreement across different Reynolds numbers confirms that the observed scaling is a genuine reflection of the turbulent flow physics rather than an artifact of a particular operating condition.

The consistency between experiment and the Kolmogorov-based model validates both the theoretical framework and the effective-temperature interpretation. It demonstrates that the string faithfully transduces the scale-dependent statistics of the turbulent drag forces into measurable mechanical fluctuations.

## Conclusion

Our results establish the vibrating string as a viable and effective tool for probing turbulent flows in a scale-resolved manner. By harnessing the string's harmonic modes as scale-selective sensors and interpreting their fluctuations through a fluctuation-dissipation framework, we obtain a global measurement that nonetheless retains sensitivity to individual turbulent scales. The strong agreement with the Kolmogorov-based prediction of a -11/3 spectral exponent, sustained across a broad range of Reynolds numbers, underscores the reliability and physical soundness of the approach.

This technique opens promising avenues for future studies of turbulence, offering a relatively simple experimental platform for extracting detailed spectral information. Beyond its immediate application, the framework may be extended to explore other complex flows and to further investigate the concept of effective temperature in non-equilibrium fluid systems.

# Combining Evidence: Harmonic Approaches and FDR Control in Multiple Testing

When researchers run many statistical tests at once, they face a fundamental challenge: how do you separate genuine discoveries from the noise that inevitably arises by chance? Two important tools that address this problem are the **harmonic** mean p-value and the **False Discovery Rate (FDR)**. Together, they offer complementary strategies for drawing reliable conclusions from large datasets.

## The Harmonic Mean p-Value

The harmonic mean p-value is a method for combining evidence across multiple tests. Rather than treating each result in isolation, it aggregates p-values in a way that is robust to dependence between tests—a common feature of real-world data. The harmonic approach is especially attractive because it remains valid even when the individual tests are correlated, a situation where many classical combination methods fail. This makes it a powerful option for assessing whether a group of related findings, taken as a whole, provides meaningful support for a hypothesis.

## Understanding FDR

The False Discovery Rate takes a different angle. Instead of asking whether any single result is significant, FDR controls the *expected proportion* of false positives among all the discoveries you declare. This shift in perspective is enormously useful in fields like genomics, neuroimaging, and machine learning, where thousands of comparisons may be evaluated simultaneously. By tolerating a small, controlled fraction of errors, FDR methods such as the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure allow scientists to identify many true effects without being overwhelmed by the stringency of traditional corrections.

## Why This Matters

This combination of techniques reflects a broader theme in modern statistics: balancing sensitivity against reliability. The harmonic mean approach helps summarize scattered evidence, while FDR ensures that the flood of "significant" results reported in large studies does not consist mostly of false alarms. This is not merely a technical detail—it directly affects which drugs advance to trials, which genes are flagged for further study, and which patterns are trusted enough to guide real decisions.

In an era defined by massive data, understanding tools like the harmonic mean p-value and FDR is essential. This foundation empowers researchers to move beyond raw numbers and toward conclusions that are both meaningful and trustworthy.

# Abstract

We present an experimental investigation of turbulent velocity fluctuations in a free air jet using a vibrating string as a mechanical probe. A thin string, clamped at both ends and positioned transverse to the flow, responds to the fluctuating drag forces imparted by the turbulent field, translating hydrodynamic fluctuations into measurable mechanical oscillations. By analyzing the string's displacement spectrum through optical detection, we characterize both the amplitude and frequency content of the driven motion across a range of Reynolds numbers.

We interpret the string's response within the framework of the fluctuation-dissipation relation, treating the turbulent flow as a non-equilibrium stochastic bath. From the ratio of the measured fluctuation spectrum to the dissipative response function of the string, we extract a frequency-dependent effective temperature that quantifies the intensity of the turbulent forcing. This effective temperature is found to greatly exceed the ambient thermal temperature and exhibits a systematic dependence on the mean flow velocity and the string's position within the jet, reflecting the spatial structure of the turbulent cascade.

Our results demonstrate that a vibrating string serves as a simple, robust, and spatially localized probe of turbulent statistics, and that the effective-temperature concept provides a compact, physically meaningful characterization of the driven fluctuations. We discuss the connection between the measured effective temperature and standard turbulence quantities such as the turbulent kinetic energy and dissipation rate, and comment on the applicability of fluctuation-dissipation ideas to strongly non-equilibrium hydrodynamic systems.

# Abstract

Turbulent flows exhibit fluctuation and dissipation phenomena reminiscent of thermal systems, motivating the search for an effective temperature that characterizes their statistical steady state. Here we present experimental measurements of velocity fluctuations and energy dissipation in a turbulent flow using a mechanical string probe—a flexible filament whose transverse displacements respond to the surrounding flow field. By simultaneously tracking the spontaneous fluctuations of the probe and its dissipative response to controlled perturbations, we test the applicability of a fluctuation-dissipation relation (FDR) to the turbulent state. From the ratio of the fluctuation spectrum to the imaginary part of the response function, we extract a scale-dependent effective temperature $T_{\mathrm{eff}}(\omega)$. We find that the FDR-derived temperature is approximately constant over an intermediate range of frequencies corresponding to the inertial subrange, while systematic deviations appear at both large and small scales, reflecting energy injection and viscous dissipation, respectively. We compare this FDR-based effective temperature with alternative definitions proposed in the turbulence literature, including those based on kinetic-energy equipartition, the balance of energy flux, and Lagrangian acceleration statistics. The comparison reveals both quantitative agreement within the inertial range and instructive discrepancies that illuminate the limits of thermodynamic analogies in nonequilibrium turbulence. Our results demonstrate that a mechanical string probe provides a practical tool for probing fluctuation-dissipation physics in turbulent flows and offer a unifying framework for interpreting the various notions of turbulence temperature.

---

*Keywords:* turbulence, fluctuation-dissipation relation, effective temperature, mechanical probe, nonequilibrium statistical mechanics, energy dissipation

# Abstract

We present an exploratory investigation of the fluctuation-dissipation relation (FDR) and the emergence of an effective temperature in a turbulent jet, employing a flexible string as a distributed probe whose harmonic modes are excited by fluctuating hydrodynamic drag. The string, transversely mounted within the developed region of a turbulent axisymmetric jet, responds to the stochastic velocity field through drag-induced forcing, transforming its normal modes into a spectrum of driven-damped oscillators. By treating each harmonic as an independent degree of freedom, we test whether the response and correlation functions of the string satisfy a generalized fluctuation-dissipation relation, thereby permitting the definition of a mode-dependent effective temperature that characterizes the non-equilibrium energy injection by the turbulence.

Building on Kolmogorov's 1941 (K41) phenomenology, we derive scaling predictions for the modal energy distribution and the effective temperature as functions of wavenumber, linking the inertial-range statistics of the turbulent forcing to the spectral response of the string. In particular, the K41 framework predicts a characteristic power-law dependence of the effective temperature on mode number, reflecting the underlying energy cascade and the frequency content of the drag fluctuations.

Experimental measurements of the string's transverse displacement, obtained via high-speed imaging and modal decomposition, are compared against these predictions. We find that the low-order harmonics exhibit an effective temperature consistent with K41 scaling over an intermediate range of modes, while deviations at high wavenumbers are attributed to dissipative and finite-size effects. Our results demonstrate that a driven string constitutes a simple yet quantitative probe of non-equilibrium statistical mechanics in turbulence, and that the effective-temperature concept provides a useful bridge between the fluctuation-dissipation formalism and the classical scaling theory of turbulent flows.
